newsitem.title: USA: Senator predicts tough CIA confirmation hearings.
newsitem.headline: Senator predicts tough CIA confirmation hearings.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice to be his third director of central intelligence, Anthony Lake, faces "tough sailing" in Senate confirmation hearings, the head of the Senate Budget Committee predicted on Sunday.
Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, voiced qualms about Lake, who is now national security adviser, as the proposed replacement for John Deutch, the director of central intelligence.
"I think the Senate thought John Deutch was doing a pretty good job and all of a sudden, unceremoniously, he's replaced in a kind of in-house coup," Domenici said on the CNN programme "Late Edition."

Predicting how Lake's confirmation hearings would go before the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, Domenici responded, "Tough sailing, in my opinion." Nevertheless, Lake, 57, is widely expected to be confirmed as top U.S. spymaster.

Clinton nominated Lake on Thursday as part of a revamped national security team for his second term. He tapped Madeleine Albright, now the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, to be secretary of state, Sen. William Cohen to be defence secretary and Samuel Berger, Lake's deputy, to take over as national security adviser.

"I think of the four, the one that's most apt to get some congressional criticism and that it might be a little tough on is the CIA director (Lake) because I think the Senate thought John Deutch was doing a pretty good job," Domenici said.

Deutch, a former Pentagon number two man who has been CIA director for 20 months, had hoped to become Clinton's next secretary of defence, according to friends. He told the New York Times last week that he "would have stayed on at some post" had it been offered.

Reservations about Lake in some quarters are based on his lack of experience managing a sprawling bureaucracy, let alone one as rough and tumble as the Central Intelligence Agency and its 12 companion spy outfits in the executive branch.
Former Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger said he believed the CIA had failed to pay enough attention to recruiting spies and was in "bad shape."
"It needs reform and I'm not sure Tony Lake is strong enough to do it," he said on CNN.

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a New York Democrat who is a former vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said the CIA was "too big for its own good and John Deutch has been taking on some of those issues."

R. James Woolsey, Clinton's first CIA chief, predicted Lake would find it "hard, not impossible, but hard" to pass critical judgments on policies that he himself helped craft in his old national security adviser's job.

"Essentially, being director of central intelligence is a skunk-at-the-garden-party job," he said on the same programme. "You're always telling people things they don't want to hear, sometimes that their policies aren't working."
